title: Higher-order quantum thermodynamics: equilibrium and causal structure
authors: Simon Milz, Kyrylo Simonov, Zoltán Zimborás, Tamal Guha, Saptarshi Roy, Giulio Chiribella
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics is traditionally formulated as a theory of equilibrium states and state transformations. Recent advances in higher-order quantum transformations, which describe physical scenarios beyond states and channels and provide a systematic framework for causal order, raise the question of how equilibrium should be defined and preserved in this more general setting. Starting from the Gibbs state as the unique equilibrium state, we identify equilibrium preservation as its natural higher-order extension. We show that, while this principle can in general give rise to distinct classes of transformations, all such distinctions disappear when equilibrium preservation is required completely, namely under arbitrary ancillary extensions. Remarkably, every transformation satisfying this condition is causally ordered, making causal order an emergent consequence of thermodynamic equilibrium. We establish this result for arbitrary higher-order maps and use the resulting framework to introduce free-energy-like quantities for quantum channels. Our findings reveal a fundamental connection between thermodynamic equilibrium and causal structure, providing a foundation for a fully fledged theory of higher-order quantum thermodynamics.
summary: This paper develops a theory of higher-order quantum thermodynamics by extending the concept of equilibrium preservation to multi-time processes. The central finding is that enforcing thermodynamic equilibrium constraints on these higher-order maps forces the underlying physical processes to possess a definite causal order. This establishes causality as a fundamental consequence of thermodynamic equilibrium.
main_problem: The paper addresses defining and understanding thermodynamic equilibrium and its preservation when extending quantum thermodynamics to higher-order transformations beyond simple states and channels.
main_result: It establishes that requiring complete preservation of thermodynamic equilibrium forces any transformation to be causally ordered, demonstrating that causality emerges naturally from the principle of thermodynamic equilibrium.
method: The authors use the Gibbs state as the unique equilibrium point and impose the constraint that higher-order transformations must preserve this equilibrium state under arbitrary ancillary extensions.
model_or_system: The framework analyzes quantum systems using quantum states, quantum channels (CPTP maps), and generalized higher-order transformations described by supermaps. The equilibrium state is defined by the Gibbs state $\tau = e^{-\beta\hat{H}/Z}$.
key_observables: Gibbs state ($\tau$), higher-order transformations (supermaps), causal order, and free-energy-like quantities for quantum channels.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($\beta$), Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}$), and the structure of the ancillary extensions.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a unique Gibbs equilibrium state and relies on extending physical constraints (like equilibrium preservation) to the higher-order map structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of equilibrium processes, showing state transformations ($\tau$) and supermaps ($S$) that preserve the Gibbs state, and detail the structure of superchannels via auxiliary spaces.
paper_structure: The paper systematically builds the theory from state transformations to supermaps, first defining equilibrium preservation, then showing that complete preservation implies causal ordering, and finally applying this to introduce free-energy-like quantities for channels.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical link between fundamental concepts in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (thermodynamics) and fundamental principles of quantum information theory (causality), which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Equilibrium processes. (top) To transform quantum states, an experimenter receives a thermodynamic system in a state 𝜌(depicted by the charged battery) and manipulates it via a trans- formation G, depleting free energy (depicted by the discharged bat- tery). We consider such a process "in equilibrium", if it preserves the Gibbs state 𝜏, leading to the set of GP and GPTP transforma- tions (see Sec. II C). (bottom) Similarly, an equilibrium supermap S transforms state transformations, leaving the set of Gibbs-preserving transformations invariant. This requirement leads to several possible inequivalent sets of equilibrium supermaps (GPP, GPTPP, CGPP, CGPTPP, see Sec. III A)....

Figure 2. The basic type of quantum supermap. The basic type of quantum supermap S (depicted in magenta) transforms a quantum channel/operation T with input 𝐼and output 𝑂(light blue on the left side of the equality sign), into a new quantum channel/operation T ′ with input 𝑃and output 𝐹(light blue on the right side of the equality sign).
Figure 3. CP supermaps. A supermap S is CP if the map S ⊗I𝑎→𝑏 transforms CP maps T ∈CP(𝐼⊗𝑎,𝑂⊗𝑏) to CP maps T ′ ∈CP(𝑃⊗ 𝑎, 𝐹⊗𝑏) for every possible pair of finite-dimensional systems 𝑎and 𝑏.

Figure 4. Structure of superchannels. Any proper supermap S : CPTP(𝐼,𝑂) →CPTP(𝑃, 𝐹) can be obtained via the concatenation of two CPTP maps E : L(H𝑃) →L(H𝐼⊗H𝑐) and D : L(H𝑂⊗ H𝑐) →L(H𝐹), where H𝑐is an auxiliary space representing memory. Whenever a supermap can be realized via an underlying circuit, we will denote the temporal order of occurrence of spaces by the ≺ symbol, i.e., for this superchannel we have 𝑃≺𝐼≺𝑂≺𝐹.

Figure 5. Higher-order transformation from a quantum circuit. Different users (here, Alice, Bob, Charlie and Dave) in a distributed quantum computation – schematically given by a circuit with unit- aries U1, U2, and U3 – can perform manipulations X ∈CP(𝐼𝑋,𝑂𝑋) on different qubits at different points in time. The overall action of the circuit onto the corresponding operations is given by a higher- order transformation W, such that K = W[A, B, C, D] ∈CP(𝑃, 𝐹). Here, W is causally ordered – since it stems from a quantum circuit. More generally, higher-order transformations can also account for causally indefinite correlations between different operations.
